scenario.title: Support backlog
scenario.initial_request: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

M-REFUND-FAILURE-COUNT.name: Count of refund records with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT in payment-db
M-REFUND-FAILURE-COUNT.measurement_window: all refund_failures records returned by payment-db at time of query

M-TICKET-RESPONSE-MEDIAN.name: Median ticket response time vs SLA

M-REFUND-COMPLETION-RATE.name: Share of attempted refunds that complete successfully

F-01.statement: payment-db refund_failures returned 5 records, all with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT.

F-02.statement: ticket-db response_times shows median response time 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets.

CL-01.statement: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

CL-02.statement: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

H-SLOW-RESPONSE.statement: Customers experience backlog because they lack a fast self-service channel for refund status, so a chatbot answering refund queries would resolve the backlog.

H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY.statement: The backlog is driven by actual delays in refund payment processing (DA-PAY), so customers wait because refunds are genuinely slow, not because they lack information access.

H-STAFFING-CAPACITY-SHORTAGE.statement: Support backlog stems from insufficient staff capacity relative to ticket volume, not from lack of self-service answers.

H-TICKET-VOLUME-POLICY-CONFUSI.statement: High ticket volume is driven by unclear refund policy or process steps causing repeat/duplicate contacts, inflating the apparent backlog.

H-AGENT-DATA-VISIBILITY-GAP.statement: Support agents lack timely visibility into refund payment status, causing them to delay responses to customers even though the information exists in DA-PAY.

H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE.statement: Refunds fail processing because recorded IBANs are in an invalid format (FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), requiring manual correction and causing the response/refund backlog.

interpretation_history.interpretation: All 5 refund_failures records in payment-db (E-01) show status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, indicating refunds are genuinely stuck in payment processing due to a data-format problem, not merely waiting or hidden from view.

Ticket-db response_times shows a median response time of 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets, indicating that on aggregate most support tickets are answered well within SLA. This undermines the framing that customers broadly "wait" for refund answers due to slow agent response.

E-03.content: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

interpretation_history.interpretation: SH-SUP's interview answer restates the initial request framing already captured in CL-01 (customers wait, a chatbot would fix it); it is a non-authoritative, incomplete stakeholder opinion that adds no new causal evidence and is consistent with the stakeholder's recorded bias toward framing the issue as response speed.

U-IBAN-ROOT-CAUSE.question: Does the invalid IBAN format originate from customer data entry, a ticket-intake form, or an internal system/integration defect?
U-IBAN-ROOT-CAUSE.decision_impact: Determines whether the fix is a one-time data correction, an upstream validation feature, or both.
U-IBAN-ROOT-CAUSE.resolution_path: Trace the lineage of the 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records back through DA-TCK/DA-PAY intake to find where IBAN values were captured.
U-IBAN-ROOT-CAUSE.safe_placeholder: Manually correct the 5 known failed records now; defer any upstream validation change until lineage is confirmed.

U-BACKLOG-FULL-SCOPE.question: Do the 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records represent the entire current refund backlog, or only a partial view, given DA-PAY completeness is UNKNOWN?
U-BACKLOG-FULL-SCOPE.decision_impact: Changes whether a success criterion of '0 failed records' actually closes the backlog or only addresses a fraction of it.
U-BACKLOG-FULL-SCOPE.resolution_path: Query payment-db.refund_failures across the full relevant time range/all statuses to confirm the total count.
U-BACKLOG-FULL-SCOPE.safe_placeholder: Report success against the known backlog of 5 records only and keep backlog-scope verification open rather than claiming full resolution.

U-TICKET-VOLUME-DRIVER.question: Is refund-related ticket volume partly inflated by unclear refund policy/process steps (H-TICKET-VOLUME-POLICY-CONFUSI), independent of the IBAN processing failure?
U-TICKET-VOLUME-DRIVER.decision_impact: Would justify adding policy-clarification scope beyond the IBAN fix.
U-TICKET-VOLUME-DRIVER.resolution_path: Analyze ticket-db content/tags for repeat-contact or policy-confusion markers.
U-TICKET-VOLUME-DRIVER.safe_placeholder: Keep policy-clarification out of scope until analysis confirms a distinct driver.

A-SAMPLE-REPRESENTATIVENESS.statement: The 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records returned by payment-db are treated as the current refund backlog needing correction, even though DA-PAY completeness is marked UNKNOWN.

A-IBAN-CAUSE-SUFFICIENT.statement: Correcting IBAN format is assumed sufficient to resolve the observed backlog, since E-01 shows a single uniform failure status across all 5 records with no other failure types present.

SC-IBAN-FIX.statement: All refund records currently failing due to invalid IBAN format are corrected and successfully reprocessed.
SC-IBAN-FIX.validation_method: Re-run payment-db.refund_failures query and confirm no record has status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT.

SC-SLA-MAINTAINED.statement: Ticket response times continue to meet the 24-hour SLA while the refund fix is implemented.
SC-SLA-MAINTAINED.validation_method: Re-run ticket-db.response_times query and confirm median_hours <= sla_hours.

problem_definition.requested_solution: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds.
symptoms: 5 of 5 observed refund records in payment-db show status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01), i.e. refunds genuinely stuck in processing.
Stakeholder SH-SUP reports customers 'wait forever' for refund answers and attributes this to lack of self-service (CL-01, CL-02, E-03).
problem_definition.root_problem: Refunds are failing in payment processing because recorded IBANs are in an invalid format (payment-db shows 5 of 5 observed refund_failures as FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), creating a backlog of unresolved refunds; this is not caused by slow or missing customer-facing answers, since ticket-db shows a 2.0-hour median response time against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets.

structural_remedies.description: Re-run/expand the payment-db refund_failures query and seek a completeness attestation to establish whether the 5 records represent the entire backlog.

decision_log.rationale: causal chain: Refund records contain IBAN values in an invalid format (E-01). → Payment processing rejects these refund transactions, recording status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT for all 5 observed records (E-01). → Rejected refunds remain uncorrected and unresolved, accumulating as a backlog of failed refunds in DA-PAY (E-01). → Support ticket responses stay well within SLA (median 2.0h vs 24h across 900 tickets, E-02), so the backlog is not explained by slow agent replies to customers. → Customers experience unresolved refunds as 'waiting', which the requesting stakeholder (SH-SUP) frames as a response-speed problem (E-03/CL-02), but the underlying cause is stuck payment transactions, not answer latency.; rejected framings: [('H-SLOW-RESPONSE', "Contradicted by E-01 (refunds are genuinely stuck in processing, not merely unanswered) and E-02 (median ticket response of 2.0h vs 24h SLA shows agents respond fast); rests only on stakeholder claims E-03/CL-02 that repeat the initial request's framing."), ('H-AGENT-DATA-VISIBILITY-GAP', 'Status REJECTED, contradicted by E-01 and E-02; no evidence agents lack visibility into DA-PAY.'), ('H-STAFFING-CAPACITY-SHORTAGE', 'Status REJECTED, contradicted by E-02 which shows tickets handled well within SLA, indicating no staffing capacity shortfall.')]
[CONDITIONAL] critical unknown U-IBAN-ROOT-CAUSE deferred to VOB-U-IBAN-ROOT-CAUSE; [CONDITIONAL] critical unknown U-BACKLOG-FULL-SCOPE deferred to VOB-U-BACKLOG-FULL-SCOPE

actions.question: What do actual refund payment failure/delay records in DA-PAY show about processing times and failure rates for the backlog period?
actions.expected_information_gain: Reveals whether refunds are genuinely delayed/failing at the payment-processing layer, which would support H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY over the chatbot-fix hypotheses (H-SLOW-RESPONSE, H-AGENT-DATA-VISIBILITY-GAP).
actions.decision_impact_rationale: H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY is CRITICAL decision_impact; if true, a chatbot cannot fix the root cause and the next decision (reject/redirect the chatbot proposal) changes entirely.
actions.why_now: CL-01 (refund_backlog.root_cause) is UNVERIFIED and DA-PAY completeness is UNKNOWN; this is the only direct evidence source for whether the backlog is a payment-processing problem rather than a communication problem.

actions.question: What do ticket volume and response-time records in DA-TCK show: are tickets duplicated/repeat contacts, and is response delay correlated with ticket volume versus agent-side information gaps?
actions.expected_information_gain: Distinguishes whether the backlog is driven by sheer volume (staffing shortage), repeat/duplicate contacts (policy confusion), or slow agent responses despite low volume (self-service or visibility gap).
actions.decision_impact_rationale: Directly tests three competing HIGH/MEDIUM-impact hypotheses (staffing, policy confusion, slow response) that each imply a different fix than a chatbot.
actions.why_now: DA-TCK completeness is UNKNOWN and no evidence yet exists on ticket patterns; this is needed before any decision on chatbot scope can be made.

actions.question: Can SH-SUP provide concrete examples or metrics behind the claim that 'customers wait for answers about refunds' (CL-01), e.g. typical wait causes, staffing levels, or policy ambiguity?
actions.expected_information_gain: May surface qualitative detail (e.g. known staffing gaps or policy complaints) not visible in the two data queries, but SH-SUP's noted bias toward framing everything as response speed limits how much it can discriminate root cause.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: CL-01 is the only basis for the chatbot request and is UNVERIFIED; clarifying it could still adjust scope, but less decisively than the two data queries given the stakeholder's stated bias.
actions.why_now: SH-SUP is the sole source of CL-01 and the initial request; probing further before committing budget to a chatbot build is low-cost relative to the decision at stake, though data queries should take priority given the known framing bias.

proposal.root_problem: Refunds are failing in payment processing because recorded IBANs are in an invalid format (payment-db shows 5 of 5 observed refund_failures as FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), creating a backlog of unresolved refunds; this is not caused by slow or missing customer-facing answers, since ticket-db shows a 2.0-hour median response time against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets.
proposal.requested_solution: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds.
symptoms: 5 of 5 observed refund records in payment-db show status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01), i.e. refunds genuinely stuck in processing.
Stakeholder SH-SUP reports customers 'wait forever' for refund answers and attributes this to lack of self-service (CL-01, CL-02, E-03).
causal_chain: Refund records contain IBAN values in an invalid format (E-01).
Payment processing rejects these refund transactions, recording status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT for all 5 observed records (E-01).
Rejected refunds remain uncorrected and unresolved, accumulating as a backlog of failed refunds in DA-PAY (E-01).
Support ticket responses stay well within SLA (median 2.0h vs 24h across 900 tickets, E-02), so the backlog is not explained by slow agent replies to customers.

Customers experience unresolved refunds as 'waiting', which the requesting stakeholder (SH-SUP) frames as a response-speed problem (E-03/CL-02), but the underlying cause is stuck payment transactions, not answer latency.

assumptions.statement: The 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records returned by payment-db are treated as the current refund backlog needing correction, even though DA-PAY completeness is marked UNKNOWN.

key_points: Problem as defined (PD-1): the backlog's root cause is refund processing failure, not slow customer answers — payment-db shows all 5 observed refund records with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01/F-01), while ticket-db shows a 2.0-hour median response time against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets (E-02/F-02).

This root cause was established by testing competing hypotheses: H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE was CONFIRMED (supported by E-01), while H-SLOW-RESPONSE, H-STAFFING-CAPACITY-SHORTAGE and H-AGENT-DATA-VISIBILITY-GAP were REJECTED (contradicted by E-01/E-02); the stakeholder's chatbot framing (CL-01, CL-02, E-03) was treated as an unverified claim, not fact.

The stakeholder's original request ('build a chatbot') and restated claim (CL-02, E-03) attribute the backlog to lack of self-service, but this is non-authoritative stakeholder opinion (E-03) that the evidence contradicts; conflicts C-1 and C-2 (root_cause disagreement between E-01 and CL-02/E-03) were documented but remain formally OPEN.

The DEFINE gate returned CONDITIONAL_PASS, deferring two critical unknowns (U-IBAN-ROOT-CAUSE, U-BACKLOG-FULL-SCOPE) to verification obligations VOB-U-IBAN-ROOT-CAUSE and VOB-U-BACKLOG-FULL-SCOPE, both still OPEN at release.

What was released: only the ticket-volume-driver analysis for DA-TCK (work item W-WI-1, status DONE) was in the release scope and minimum useful scope of solution design SD-1; corrective remedies such as IBAN record correction, backlog scope verification/reprocessing, root-origin tracing, and adding a validation contract were not executed and remain unfinished.

The release decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION (no holds): the two open VOBs block correction and full-scope-verification actions outside the release scope, and both payment-db and ticket-db are read-only, so this agent could not execute any corrective or validation action even if the VOBs were resolved.

Two confirmed metrics at release: M-REFUND-FAILURE-COUNT = 5 (FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records, E-01) and M-TICKET-RESPONSE-MEDIAN = 2.0 hours against a 24-hour target (E-02); M-REFUND-COMPLETION-RATE has no current value.
limitations_explained: DA-PAY (payment-db) completeness is marked UNKNOWN, so the true scope of the refund backlog beyond the 5 known FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records is unverified; this status may not change without an authoritative attestation from the source-system owner, leaving VOB-U-BACKLOG-FULL-SCOPE formally open regardless of re-querying.

No data asset describes the customer-entry/ticket-intake/internal-integration layer, so it is not known where invalid IBAN formats originate; VOB-U-IBAN-ROOT-CAUSE cannot be closed within this release and requires an external engineering/payment-ops handoff.

Both payment-db and ticket-db are read-only tools, so no corrective action (correcting IBAN records, reprocessing refunds) or validation-contract change can be executed by this agent regardless of findings.

The process/data-lineage review to localize where invalid IBAN formats are introduced, and the IBAN-format validation rule/contract to prevent future failures, remain unfinished and were not performed in this release.

Conflicts C-1 (E-01 vs CL-02) and C-2 (E-01 vs E-03) over the root-cause assertion remain OPEN; although remedy SR-R-REFRAME-STAKEHOLDER documents the IBAN-failure conclusion, this release does not formally close those conflicts.
The DEFINE gate result was CONDITIONAL_PASS rather than a full pass, because the two critical unknowns above were deferred to verification obligations instead of being resolved before release.
proposal.summary: The requester (SH-SUP) framed the problem as customers waiting for refund answers and proposed a chatbot, but the problem as formally defined (PD-1) is that refunds are failing in payment processing due to invalid IBAN format: payment-db shows all 5 observed refund_failures records as FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01), while ticket-db shows a healthy 2.0-hour median response time against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets (E-02), rejecting the slow-response/self-service framing (hypotheses H-SLOW-RESPONSE, H-STAFFING-CAPACITY-SHORTAGE, H-AGENT-DATA-VISIBILITY-GAP all REJECTED; H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE CONFIRMED). The DEFINE gate returned CONDITIONAL_PASS because two critical unknowns (whether the 5 records represent the full backlog, and where the IBAN defect originates) were deferred as open verification obligations rather than resolved. Given this, the release only delivered the ticket-volume-driver analysis on DA-TCK (W-WI-1); no corrective IBAN-fix, backlog-scope verification, or validation-contract work was executed, both because the relevant VOBs remain open and outside release scope and because the underlying payment-db/ticket-db tools are read-only. The decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION with no holds, documenting these gaps as known limitations rather than resolving them.
